{{Short description|Condition for control system stability}}

In [[control theory]], the '''Liénard–Chipart criterion''' is a [[stability criterion]] modified from the [[Routh–Hurwitz stability criterion]], proposed in 1914 by French physicists [[Alfred-Marie Liénard|A. Liénard]] and M. H. Chipart.<ref name="LC14" >{{cite journal |last1=Liénard |first1=A. |last2=Chipart |first2=M. H. |year=1914 |title=Sur le signe de la partie réelle des racines d'une équation algébrique |journal=[[Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées|J. Math. Pures Appl.]] |volume=10 |issue=6 |pages=291–346 }}</ref> This criterion has a computational advantage over the Routh–Hurwitz criterion because it involves only about half the number of [[determinant]] computations.<ref name="Gantmacher">{{cite book |author=Felix Gantmacher |url= |title=The Theory of Matrices |publisher=American Mathematical Society |year=2000 |isbn=0-8218-2664-6 |volume=2 |pages=221–225 |author-link=Felix Gantmacher}}</ref>

== Algorithm ==

The Routh–Hurwitz stability criterion says that a [[necessary and sufficient]] condition for all the [[zero of a function|roots]] of the [[polynomial]] with [[real number|real]] [[coefficient]]s

<math display=block>f(z) = a_0 z^n + a_1 z^{n-1} + \cdots + a_n, \quad a_0 > 0 </math>

to have negative real parts (i.e. {{mvar|f}} is Hurwitz [[Stable polynomial|stable]]) is that

<math display=block> \Delta_1 > 0,\, \Delta_2 > 0, \ \ldots, \ \Delta_n > 0, </math>

where {{math|&Delta;{{sub|''i''}}}} is the {{mvar|i}}-th [[Minor (linear algebra)#Other applications|leading principal minor]] of the [[Routh–Hurwitz matrix|Hurwitz matrix]] associated with {{mvar|f}}.

Using the same notation as above, the Liénard–Chipart criterion is that {{mvar|f}} is Hurwitz stable if and only if any one of the four conditions is satisfied:

<math display=block>\begin{align}
  1) \quad& a_n > 0,\ a_{n-2} > 0,\ a_{n-4} > 0,\ \ldots \\
          &\Delta_1 > 0,\ \Delta_3 > 0,\ \ldots \\[4pt]
  2) \quad& a_n > 0,\ a_{n-2} > 0,\ a_{n-4} > 0,\ \ldots \\
          & \Delta_2 > 0,\ \Delta_4 > 0,\ \ldots \\[4pt]
  3) \quad& a_n > 0,\ a_{n-1} > 0,\ a_{n-3} > 0,\ \ldots \\
           &\Delta_1 > 0,\ \Delta_3 > 0,\ \ldots \\[4pt]
  4) \quad& a_n > 0,\ a_{n-1} > 0,\ a_{n-3}  > 0,\ \ldots \\
          &\Delta_2 > 0,\ \Delta_4 > 0,\ \ldots
\end{align}</math>

Hence one can see that by choosing one of these conditions, the number of determinants required to be evaluated is reduced.

Alternatively Fuller formulated this as follows for (noticing that {{math|&Delta;{{sub|1}} > 0}} is never needed to be checked):

<math display=block>\begin{align}
  & a_n > 0,\ a_1 > 0,\ a_3 > 0,\ a_5 > 0,\  \ldots; \\  
  & \Delta_{n-1} > 0,\ \Delta_{n-3} > 0,\ \Delta_{n-5} > 0,\ \ldots,\ 
    \begin{cases} 
      n \text{ even} & \Delta_3 > 0 \\ 
      n \text{ odd} & \Delta_2 > 0
    \end{cases}
\end{align}</math> 

This means if {{mvar|n}} is even, the second line ends in {{math|&Delta;{{sub|3}} > 0}} and if {{mvar|n}} is odd, it ends in {{math|&Delta;{{sub|2}} > 0}} and so this is just condition (2) for odd {{mvar|n}} and  condition (3) for even {{mvar|n}} from above. The first line always ends in {{mvar|a{{sub|n}}}}, but {{math|''a''{{sub|''n''-1}} > 0}} is also needed for even {{mvar|n}}.
